newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico opposition sees harsh lesson in drug scandal.
newsitem.headline: Mexico opposition sees harsh lesson in drug scandal.

text.p: Mexico's worst drug scandal in years shows how rotten the country's one-party political system has become, Mexican opposition leaders are charging.

Stunned by the arrest and imprisonment of the country's top anti-drug official on charges of collaborating with a cocaine king, politicians and analysts asked how many other corrupt top brass remained in Mexico's military.
"This has caused a very serious institutional crisis," said Felipe Calderon Hinojosa, president of the main opposition party, the conservative National Action Party (PAN).
"This is the most serious symptom of the decomposition and the corruption in the corridors of power in Mexico in recent years," he told foreign correspondents on Wednesday night.

After just two months in the job, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo was fired on Monday as head of the National Institute for Drug Combat (INCD) after the government said he took payoffs from the country's top drug lord Amado Carrillo Fuentes in return for information and protection.
In Washington, President Bill Clinton expressed concern over the corruption case but said he was pleased the Mexican government had "not fooled around" in dealing with it.
"It's a very serious revelation and deeply troubling," Clinton told reporters after an unrelated White House event.
"They're obviously saying to the world and the people of Mexico, we will not tolerate the corruption if we find it and root it out, even if it's at the highest level," he said.
Mexico's Attorney-General Jorge Madrazo said other military officers were under investigation and that further arrests were possible, though he declined to give names.
The scandal was acutely painful for Mexicans who had believed that the army -- whose image here is better than in many other Latin American countries -- was one of their few honest institutions.

It also followed lurid allegations by two local media that former president Carlos Salinas de Gortari and his family attended parties with another top drug trafficker, Juan Garcia Abrego, and took his money in return for protection during Salinas's 1988-94 administration.

Salinas and his jailed brother Raul strongly denied the allegations. But left-wing opposition party leader Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador said those charges were "another sign of the decomposition of the regime which indicates that there is a very severe political crisis".

One radio station, Radio Red, did a quick survey of street opinion and found most citizens wanted the general to go before a firing squad for treason. The government says he will first face a civil trial on charges of racketeering.

A senior PAN official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Reuters: "My biggest worry is that this is the tip of an iceberg. We haven't heard anything about the navy or the air force, for example, and we know that most drugs here are shipped by sea."

Echoing that concern, political commentator Sergio Sarmiento recalled in a column on Thursday headlined "Narco-Politics" that during the Salinas administration a top admiral had been fired without explanation amid rumours of drug trafficking. The admiral was never charged.

Aides to President Zedillo said one rotten apple would not affect the government's commitment to the war on drugs but politicians from other parties saw the scandal as a metaphor for the seediness bred by a one-party system.
Mexico has been ruled since 1929 by a single party and political analysts say its domination over most aspects of national life has fostered rampant corruption and weakened institutions.

Miguel Angel Granados Chapa, a left-leaning political commentator, said Mexicans had always mistakenly placed too much trust in the military. Gen. Alvaro Obregon, a hero of the 1910 Mexican Revolution, used to say "there is not a general who can resist a cannon shot of 50,000 pesos," he recalled.
